# Abstract {.unnumbered}

<!-- ≤ 350 words, one paragraph, no citations. Topic keywords (decision support,
reef interventions, scaling) in the first two sentences. -->

Reef interventions are moving from field trials to program-scale operations, where their efficiency depends on decision support that works at the scales where crews and managers act. Control of crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) on the Great Barrier Reef is one such intervention, and it poses two recurring decisions: where on a reef to search and cull, and how to allocate control among connected reefs. We ranked all `r int(n_sites)` designated cull sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs by combining 30 m habitat models with recent cull dives and manta tows, and evaluated the ranking on held-out data against no-information baselines at equal effort. Habitat alone ranked locations within reefs weakly (within reef-year AUC `r a2(auc_lo)`–`r a2(auc_hi)`). Deferring the lowest-ranked fifth of sites retained `r p1(oc("high_retained"))` of dives above 0.04 COTS per minute, against `r p1(oc("high_retained", "random"))` at random, but avoided no more low-density dives than random selection. Ranking became more useful when applied only where evidence was weak. We replayed `r int(pdtot$visits)` reef visits from 2020–2026 under a workflow that kept previously productive sites and strong manta evidence and ranked only the remaining dives, using priority classes scaled by recent reef density and each site's record. It avoided `r p1(crv("ghost_avoided_pct"))` of empty dives and missed `r p1(crv("high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04; skipping the same number at random avoided `r p1(crd("ghost_avoided_pct"))` and missed `r p1(crd("high_missed_pct"))`. For manta surveillance, evenly spaced tows retained more aggregations than model-ranked tows, although towing only higher-ranked ground on follow-up visits saved `r p0(ccv("tows_saved_follow_up_pct"))` of those tows. For strategic decisions, we developed a site-resolved COTS–coral metacommunity model for 2,895 sub-reef sites on 113 reefs around Lizard Island. It reproduced the broad sequence of historical outbreak waves, placed past peaks within two years on two reefs outside its calibration, and supports exploratory effort scenarios to 2050, but overestimated recent densities and is not fully validated. These retrospective results cannot show what undived sites held; field trials are needed to measure realized savings. The workflow offers a testable route from fine-scale models to operational decisions.

**Keywords:** crown-of-thorns starfish, decision support, reef interventions, species distribution model, metacommunity model, outbreak control, scaling strategies, Great Barrier Reef

**Word count:** `r int(wc$main + wc$methods)` (main text). **Figures:** 9. **Tables:** 7.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Introduction

Coral reefs are declining under cumulative pressures, and keeping them functional increasingly depends on active interventions, from pest control and restoration to spatial management, delivered at scales far beyond the plots where they were first tested [@anthony2017interventions]. Scaling an intervention changes the problem it has to solve. In a trial, the question is whether the intervention works where it is applied. At program scale, much of the cost lies in deciding where and when to apply it, and those decisions are made by crews and managers at scales of tens of meters to tens of kilometers. Decision support can sharpen those choices, but only if it is built at the scale of the decision and judged against what operators would achieve without it.

Control of crown-of-thorns starfish (*Acanthaster* cf. *solaris*; COTS) on the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) is one of the few reef interventions already operating at that scale. Outbreaks of COTS have been a major cause of coral loss on the GBR [@death2012decline; @pratchett2017thirty], and the COTS Control Program suppresses them by manual culling, which reduces COTS densities and protects coral when it is sustained at the right reefs [@westcott2020efficacy; @babcock2020suppressing; @matthews2024protecting]. A substantial portion of the program's vessel and diver time goes into finding COTS. Manta tow surveys, in which an observer is towed around a reef, usually along its perimeter, locate COTS and establish a reef's outbreak status. Cull crews then dive designated sites, chosen largely from manta results and from where COTS were found before. Much of this effort finds little. Of the held-out cull dives analyzed here, `r p0(cs_ghost / cs_dives)` found no COTS and a further `r p0(cs_low / cs_dives)` found them below 0.02 COTS per minute of bottom time.

Two kinds of decision determine how efficiently this effort is used, and they operate at different fine scales. Day to day, crews decide where on a reef to tow and which designated sites to dive. Their best information is what they found last season, which is rich on reefs they visit often and thin on reefs and parts of reefs they rarely search. Strategically, managers decide which reefs to treat and when. COTS larvae disperse among reefs, so an outbreak on one reef can seed others downstream, and the spread of outbreaks depends on the structure of the connectivity network [@hock2014connectivity; @hock2017resilience]. Outbreaks on the GBR have tended to begin on reefs in a northern initiation region and spread south, which has led to proposals to concentrate control there early in an outbreak cycle [@pratchett2017thirty; @babcock2020suppressing]. The same reasoning raises operational questions that the program faces every season: when to begin culling on a reef as densities rise, when to stop on a heavily affected reef, and what either choice means for the reefs it supplies with larvae.

Modeling has so far addressed these decisions at the scale of whole reefs. Reef-level distribution models have shown that larval connectivity and water quality explain much of where outbreaks occur across the GBR [@matthews2020connectivity], and hybrid machine-learning models now forecast which reefs are likely to be in outbreak in a given year [@stewart2026hybrid]. Models of intermediate complexity and reef-scale ecosystem models, including MICE, CoCoNet and ReefMod-GBR, represent COTS and coral dynamics and have been used to compare control strategies across the reef system [@morello2014model; @plaganyi2014mice; @condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative]. Because they treat each reef as a single unit, they cannot represent where on a reef COTS aggregate, where crews search, or how culling at particular sites propagates through connected reefs. Two developments now make a finer scale feasible. Coral species distribution models built from multiscale terrain variables map habitat for key coral taxa at tens of meters [@guillaume2025coral], and COTSMod, a spatially explicit metacommunity model of COTS outbreaks and coral recovery [@matthews2020cotsmod], showed how outbreaks can be simulated across connected sites. Reef ecosystem frameworks such as ADRIA, with the computationally efficient CoralBlox coral model, can now run the large numbers of scenarios that comparisons of control strategies require [@adriacalibration2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox].

Working at fine scales raises its own problem of evaluation. Fine-scale species distribution models (SDMs) can map COTS habitat at tens of meters [@elith2009sdm], but COTS control data make them hard to evaluate. Observations are preferentially sampled, because crews dive where manta tows or past experience suggest COTS are present, so a model fitted to them partly learns operator behavior and in-sample scores overstate its skill [@diggle2010preferential; @phillips2009bias]. Survey year and reef identity dominate raw probabilities, so pooled discrimination metrics reward separating outbreak reefs from quiet ones instead of ranking places within a reef [@lobo2008auc]. Credible evaluation therefore requires held-out data at the unit of the decision [@roberts2017cv] and a baseline with the same effort.

Here, we develop fine-scale models for both kinds of decision in GBR COTS control. Specifically, we ask whether (1) habitat models combined with recent cull and manta evidence can reduce manta tows and cull dives without missing aggregations or dives above the program's target of 0.04 COTS per minute; (2) such a ranking adds more value on every designated site or only on dives made on weak evidence; and (3) a site-resolved metacommunity model reproduces observed outbreak cycles, including on reefs outside its calibration. We score the rankings on held-out reefs and forward in time, against random selection at the same effort and against the triggers crews use, because a ranking that only restates what crews already know saves nothing on the water. The metacommunity model extends COTSMod and couples it to ADRIA and CoralBlox for the Lizard Island cluster within the northern initiation region, as a prerequisite for future comparisons of control strategies.

# Materials and methods

Model reporting follows the ODMAP structure for species distribution models where it applies [@zurell2020odmap]. @tbl-design summarizes the evaluation.

  Baseline = c("AUC 0.5; lift 1", "Random and systematic thinning", "Random; habitat-only ranking", "Habitat-only ranking", "Same number of dives or tows skipped at random; block thinning; evidence-only rules", "Within-reef classes at matched effort"),

## Data and response definitions

Cull dives from the COTS Control Program, covering 2002–2026, provided the site, date, number of COTS culled and bottom time for each dive. Records with missing counts or non-positive bottom time were excluded. Dives were matched to the November 2025 designated cull-site register by reef and standardized site name, with a spatial fallback to the nearest polygon within 100 m on the same reef. This matched `r p1(ccov$dive_match_rate)` of dives. The register contained `r int(n_sites)` site polygons on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs; `r int(n_ever)` sites had been dived (@fig-study).

![**Habitat sets a first search order, and the 2027 classes and tow zone turn it into decisions on each reef.** (**a**) Probability of a problematic cull site-year in 2026 from the operational habitat layer (RG + year, with the calibrated clean + year fallback where ReefGuidance layers are missing), shown as cell means at about 2.9 km with the color scale stretched over the 2nd–98th percentiles; squares mark the reefs in **b**–**e**. The inset shows the same layer at 30 m on Eyrie Reef as within-reef percentile ranks, from low (purple) to high (yellow), the form used for ranking. (**b**–**e**) 2027 density-aware site classes (second version) on Batt, Eyrie, Lady Musgrave and Big Broadhurst reefs, with the follow-up tow zone (A–C sites plus 100 m; white dashed line), manta tows in the 12 months to 31 May 2026 (cyan: strong evidence, meaning a COTS sighting, two or more counted feeding scars or scars recorded as common) and exploration zones (purple; nested bands of each reef's top 40, 30, 20 and 10% of habitat away from cull sites and recent tows). The maps illustrate the rules and do not show measured performance on these reefs. Imagery: one Sentinel-2 true-color scene per reef (`r paste(sort(unique(substr(s2img$date, 1, 4))), collapse = ", ")`); contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data.](../outputs/figures/fig35_manuscript_gbr_and_workflow.png){#fig-study width="100%"}

Catch per unit effort (CPUE) was COTS culled per minute of bottom time. Ghost dives found no COTS, and low-density dives had positive CPUE below 0.02. The habitat models and rankings were fitted to a problematic-dive response of CPUE ≥ 0.02. Operational performance was then assessed against dives strictly above 0.04, the program's ecological target where coral cover is below 40% [@plaganyi2020targets], without refitting any model to that higher threshold. Dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive formed a separate intermediate group of useful culling opportunities.

The manta-trained model used `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "tows"))` labeled tows in `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "reef_years"))` reef-years, including `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "strong_tows"))` with strong COTS evidence. Strong evidence meant a direct COTS sighting, at least two counted feeding scars, or scars recorded as "common" in legacy surveys. Strict negatives recorded neither COTS nor scars; weak single-scar records were excluded from model fitting. Tow records came from Control Program crews (2016 onward), the Reef Joint Field Management Program (2012 onward) and the AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program (1992 onward). Scooter-assisted large area diver-based surveys (SALAD) [@pratchett2022salad] and Reef Health and Impact Surveys (RHIS) [@beeden2014rhis] contributed to the explanatory joint model only.

## Habitat predictors

All habitat predictors were assembled on a common 30 m grid in GDA2020 / MGA zone 55 and masked to within 1 km of mapped GBR and Torres Strait reefs (Supplementary Table S1). Nine terrain variables came from the multiscale terrain set built for regional coral distribution models [@guillaume2025coral]: depth, slope, eastness, northness, bathymetric position index, vector ruggedness, sky-view factor, and plan and profile curvature, each at the 30 m analysis scale. They were derived from Allen Coral Atlas satellite-derived depth at 30 m [@li2021bathymetry]. In the Torres Strait, layers derived from Allen Coral Atlas 15 m depth, averaged to 30 m, and from the 30 m DeepReef model [@beaman2017gbr30] were merged into the GBR set, with the 15 m data preferred where both existed. Three further layers were MaxEnt habitat-suitability predictions for *Acropora hyacinthus*, *A. spathulata* and *A. tenuis* from the same study, with newer predictions merged over earlier 15 m predictions and resampled bilinearly. These twelve layers covered `r p0(pick(lcov, layer_id = "legacy_clean_year2026", col = "fraction"))` of reef-polygon cells.

Five ReefGuidance layers, depth, slope, turbidity, significant wave height and peak wave period, were reprojected from regional tiles to the same grid [@reefguide2026]. Turbidity was the Allen Coral Atlas Sentinel-2 product [@li2022turbidity], in its distributed units of 10 × FNU. The five layers covered only `r p0(pick(lcov, layer_id = "legacy_rg_year2026", col = "fraction"))` of reef-polygon cells, with coverage reduced in deeper areas. Geomorphic zones came from the GBR10 mapping [@gbrmpabathymetry2021; @gbrmpageomorphic2021; @roelfsema2021shallow].

The joint model also described terrain at several scales. The 30 m depth surface was smoothed with Gaussian kernels at five scales, from none to a standard deviation of 180 m (nominal scales of 30 to 360 m; Supplementary Table S1). Slope, eastness, northness and plan and profile curvature were recomputed from each smoothed surface. Bathymetric position and local relief, the standard deviation of depth, used circular windows with a radius of 1.5 times the scale, and at least 60 m. Each of these eight terrain families was reduced to its first principal component across the five scales, fitted on the training cells.

## Habitat models

The cull-trained models used site-years. Dives were grouped by reef, cull site, recorded position and calendar year, and a site-year was problematic when its pooled CPUE, total COTS culled divided by total bottom time, reached 0.02. Two gradient-boosted tree classifiers (XGBoost) [@chen2016xgboost] predicted this indicator. The clean + year model used the twelve full-coverage layers and survey year, and was fitted on `r int(hs("clean_year", "training_rows"))` site-years with complete predictors, `r int(hs("clean_year", "positives"))` of them problematic. The RG + year model added the five ReefGuidance layers and was fitted on `r int(hs("rg_year", "training_rows"))` site-years, `r int(hs("rg_year", "positives"))` problematic. Predictors were standardized. Each model had 1,500 trees. Tree depth, learning rate, minimum loss reduction and minimum node size were tuned over a 30-point space-filling grid by five-fold spatial-block cross-validation with 50 km blocks, keeping the setting with the highest ROC AUC (Supplementary Table S2).

Both models were predicted for survey year 2026 at every 30 m cell. Survey year carried the largest share of model gain, `r p0(hp("Year", "gain_clean_year"))` in clean + year and `r p0(hp("Year", "gain_rg_year"))` in RG + year (Supplementary Table S1). Absolute probabilities therefore mainly reflect annual prevalence, and only their ordering within a reef was used. The models learned from locations selected by crews, often following manta evidence, so their scores reflect the program's sampling footprint as well as habitat.

The primary search-planning layer used RG + year where available and clean + year elsewhere. The clean + year values were first mapped onto the RG + year scale by a linear regression on the probit scale, fitted on cells where both existed. Each 30 m cell was then ranked within its reef polygon, with map priority classes for the top 10%, 10–20% and 20–30%. Of the mapped reefs, `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "RG only"))` used RG + year alone, `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "mixed"))` mixed the two sources and `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "clean fallback only"))` used the clean fallback alone. For the held-out evaluations below, models were refitted on groups of reefs with the clean + year settings (Supplementary Table S2), which were not retuned on the evaluation reefs.

Manta-trained XGBoost models used the five ReefGuidance layers and the twelve full-coverage layers, averaged along each tow, with the same boosting settings. A model with survey year was compared with a model designed to rank locations within reef-years. For the latter, the logit of the reef-year's strong-tow proportion, with a half-count correction, entered training as a fixed offset and survey year was omitted. The offset is constant within a reef-year, so it was omitted when mapping, and the resulting map represents relative log-odds rather than an annual occurrence probability. The cull-trained and manta-trained ranks were also compared as an average rank and as separate terms in the evidence model.

The joint model, a hierarchical model of species communities (HMSC) [@ovaskainen2017hmsc; @tikhonov2020hmsc], related cull, SALAD and RHIS observations to habitat on 120 m cells. Its units were cells visited in reef-years with credible COTS evidence, either a localized positive record or a strong manta tow, so it describes habitat given that a reef is active rather than annual risk. Twelve responses were modeled jointly. Nine were binary, with a probit link: problematic and any-COTS cull dives; problematic, any-COTS and feeding-scar SALAD records; and adult and juvenile COTS and branching and tabular coral scars in RHIS. Three were continuous, with a normal distribution: log SALAD density and arcsine-transformed branching and tabular live coral cover. Response traits for survey method, COTS evidence versus coral resource, and the target cull response structured the covariate effects, and the model had no random effects.

The main component used geomorphic zone, the three coral suitability layers, turbidity, wave height, wave period and the eight multiscale terrain components. Predictors were 4 × 4 block means of the 30 m layers, with geomorphic zone taken at the cell center. Where ReefGuidance or geomorphic layers were missing, a component with the coral layers and multiscale terrain, and then one with eight of the 30 m terrain layers and the coral layers, filled the gaps after the same probit calibration onto the main component's scale. The three components were fitted on `r int(hs("hmsc_enhanced", "training_rows"))`, `r int(hs("hmsc_clean", "training_rows"))` and `r int(hs("hmsc_clean_native", "training_rows"))` cell visits; for example, `r int(hs("hmsc_enhanced", "target_rows"))` cell visits in the main component had cull dives, `r int(hs("hmsc_enhanced", "positives"))` of them problematic. Each component ran four chains of 1,000 samples (Supplementary Table S2). All three passed convergence checks, with a smallest effective sample size of `r int(min(hsum$min_ess))` against a minimum of 400, and a largest upper potential scale reduction factor of `r a3(max(hsum$max_psrf_upper))` against a maximum of 1.1. Maps used 400 posterior draws. The joint model was used to describe habitat associations and uncertainty, not to rank sites.

An additional layer represented known aggregation sites using a Gaussian kernel of the problematic rate in earlier active cull site-years (σ = 500 m), blended with HMSC habitat. History and dive effort were interpreted as records of past finds and crew targeting, not as independent habitat evidence.

## Cull-site ranking

Each designated site's score combined habitat with the preceding season's cull and nearby manta evidence through a logistic regression,

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_i &= \beta_0+\beta_H H_i+\beta_P P_i+\beta_Q Q_i+\beta_R R_i\\
&\quad+\beta_E\log(1+E_i)+\beta_M\log(1+M_i)+\beta_T\log(1+T_i),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $H_i$ is the mean habitat score inside site $i$, ranked among designated sites on its reef; $P_i$ records whether any recent dive there reached CPUE ≥ 0.02; $Q_i$ records a searched site where none did; $R_i$ is the distance-weighted proportion of nearby dives reaching 0.02; $E_i$ is the weighted count of dives; and $M_i$ and $T_i$ are weighted counts of strong-evidence and all nearby manta tows. Nearby records were weighted by a Gaussian kernel (σ = 300 m) out to 900 m. Coefficients were estimated jointly from dive outcomes (Supplementary Table S3). Sites were ordered by decreasing score within each reef, and the top 20, 50, 66 and 80% of sites formed classes A, A–B, A–C and A–D, with the remainder in class E. The score encodes crew behavior as well as habitat, because past dives and tows reflect where crews chose to work.

## Evaluation of search efficiency

Operational discrimination was measured among locations on the same reef in the same year. Within reef-year AUC compared positive and negative locations only within those groups; an AUC of 0.5 indicated no discrimination. Top-20% lift was the share of positives in the highest-ranked fifth divided by 0.2. These metrics were supplemented by the outcomes retained when effort was reduced.

For operational habitat comparisons, reefs were assigned to five folds and every reef was scored by a model refitted without any reefs in its fold [@roberts2017cv]. We refer to this as leave-reef-out validation; it is grouped five-fold validation, rather than one refit per reef. This prevented a reef's cull or manta observations from contributing to its habitat fit. A separate matched manta check scored the same `r int(mi("RG + year", "tows"))` tows in `r int(mi("RG + year", "reef_years"))` active reef-years on `r int(mi("RG + year", "reefs"))` reefs where all deployed layers were available. That check used the fitted layers and was not a substitute for the refitted operational evaluation.

Manta aggregations were connected groups of strong-evidence tow midpoints linked within 500 m in a survey (reef and date); successive links could join a group wider than 500 m. The principal aggregation analysis required at least two strong tows, with isolated records examined separately. Surveys required at least five scored tows and some strong evidence. An aggregation was retained if at least one of its tows was kept. This measured retention of observed aggregation evidence under retrospective thinning.

Each thinning strategy kept the same number of tows per survey, over retained shares from 90% to 30%. Model thinning kept the highest-scoring tows. Random thinning used the exact hypergeometric expectation of retaining at least one tow in each aggregation. Systematic thinning kept evenly spaced positions in the tow sequence, averaged over 20 starting offsets. Recorded tow order was unavailable, so sequence was approximated by bearing from the survey center. The comparison therefore concerned thinning existing surveillance, not the performance of newly designed tow routes.

Cull-site analyses ranked every designated site on a reef, including never-dived sites. Random selection supplied an exact expectation at the same number of sites per reef. Rankings were compared at matched retention, because evidence could move both problematic and low-density dives upwards, and at the fixed A–D site rule, which retains the top 80% of each reef's sites and defers class E. Outcomes at never-dived sites were unknown, so these tests could not measure COTS missed at those sites or changes in crew behavior.

Spatial tests fitted the regressions on other reef folds, with evidence for a test year drawn only from preceding seasons. For each test year from 2019 to 2026, a forward test fitted the evidence regression only on earlier dive outcomes; its habitat covariates were the reef-held-out ranks, whose fits were not restricted to earlier years. A separate deployment test refitted every model on data from before each test season, on all reefs, and refreshed the evidence to the day each voyage left port. Three pre-specified alternatives to the ranking changed the prior high-density indicator, added recency-weighted site CPUE (90-day half-life), and replaced mean habitat with its within-site 90th percentile.

The HMSC–history forecast used a separate temporal design: for each test year from 2022 to 2026, habitat models were refitted on earlier years and history used earlier active site-years only. First-visit cull site-years were compared within reef-years containing both outcomes, using habitat, prior dive effort, history and their blend. This distinguished habitat transfer from the persistence of previous finds.

Uncertainty intervals used paired bootstrap resamples of reef-years for tow and cull metrics, or surveys for aggregation retention. Operational spatial comparisons used 500 resamples; the season-by-season site-ranking test used 200. The same resampled units were used across scores to preserve paired comparisons.

## Replay of a proposed on-water workflow

The site rule above would defer every dive at a low-ranked site, including dives that crews make on fresh strong evidence. Working with the program's managers, we therefore replayed a workflow on the recorded reef visits of 2019–2026: `r int(ptot$visits)` visits with a manta survey in the 30 days before or during culling, `r int(ptot$dives)` dives at designated sites and `r int(ptot$tows)` tows. Open sites, whose last dive in the previous 365 days exceeded 0.04, were dived first, and sites within 100 m of a strong-evidence tow were dived. The ranking, refreshed to each voyage's departure, decided only the remaining dives: those after a weak-evidence tow (a single counted scar, or scars recorded as present), after only negative tows, or with no tow nearby. These were made only at sites above a class cut-off, tested at A–B, A–C and A–D (@fig-workflow).

On follow-up visits, later visits to a reef in the same season, tows were also restricted to a zone: sites in classes A–B or A–C, open sites and sites within 100 m of a strong tow on an earlier visit that season. Only runs of three or more tows outside the zone were skipped. A dive whose only nearby strong tows were skipped was counted as missed. Baselines skipped the same number of dives at random among those without strong evidence, and the same tows at random positions or as blocks of nine tows on and three off. Evidence-only rules, such as requiring two scars before diving, were scored in the same replay. Intervals resampled 300 reef-years.

![**On a follow-up visit, the ranking decides only the dives that crews would make on weak evidence.** Blue boxes are new steps; the remainder is current practice. Strong evidence means a COTS sighting, two or more counted feeding scars, or scars recorded as common. The ranking is refreshed to each voyage's departure. The figure shows the recommended settings, with density-aware classes; other cut-offs were also replayed. The workflow has not been trialed.](../outputs/figures/fig23_workflow_decision.png){#fig-workflow width="100%"}

## Density-aware priority classes

Within-reef classes give every reef the same shares of sites, so a reef with few COTS has as many A sites as a reef in active outbreak. We tested classes that respond to density. A first version kept each reef's order and shifted its class shares on the odds scale by the reef's expected density over the preceding 12 months, with reefs lacking recent records placed by a reef-level outbreak forecast [@stewart2026hybrid] and discounted because about one in five such reefs needed culling. A second version weighted each dive and tow by a 90-day half-life and expressed reef density as the product of two logistic models: the chance that a survey occasion needs culling, fitted on all survey occasions including tow-only ones, and the share of problematic dives if crews dive. On reefs with recent evidence, each site's class came from the sum of two site-level log odds, the chance that a dive there is problematic and, at half weight, the chance that the site received a problematic dive on a visit (Supplementary Table S4). A site with no recent tow took the average strong-tow rate of the reef's towed sites. Class cut-offs were calibrated so that the classes held the same pooled shares of sites as the within-reef classes, and reefs without recent evidence kept density-scaled quotas. For each test season from 2020 to 2026, models were refitted on earlier seasons only, and class sets were compared at matched effort. The half-weight on the visit model was chosen on these test seasons, so differences involving it are somewhat optimistic. After these comparisons, the second version with a dive rule at A–D and a tow zone at A–C was selected as the recommended setting for field trials.

## Seasonal products

For 2027, the selected model was fitted on `r int(src$training_dives[1])` dives from `r src$training_years[1]`, with recent evidence from 1 June 2025 to 31 May 2026. Supplementary Table S5 lists the delivered layers and products. Exploration zones were drawn from 30 m cells 0.5–16 m deep that lay more than 100 m from designated cull sites and more than 150 m from manta tows in the preceding five seasons. Within each reef, these cells formed nested bands of the top 40, 30, 20 and 10% of habitat. They shade all rarely searched ground that looks like habitat, because the habitat layers cannot reliably separate individual places within it.

## Metacommunity model and historical culling

The strategic modeling strand extended COTSMod [@matthews2020cotsmod] through the Julia package COTSMod.jl, coupled to ADRIA and the CoralBlox coral model [@cotsmodmethods2026; @adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. COTSMod.jl supplied population transitions, coral predation and larval processes; ADRIA supplied the spatial domain, disturbance forcing and scenario execution. The prototype used the Lizard Island cluster, with 2,895 sub-reef sites on 113 reefs. Historical simulations beginning in 1991 were assessed against AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program (LTMP) manta COTS and coral records on Lizard Island, Eyrie, MacGillivray and North Direction reefs. The model state was expressed as recruit, juvenile and adult densities per hectare of site area, with coral cover represented relative to habitable area.

Reef-to-reef larval flows, derived from annual connectivity matrices, were divided evenly among sites within a receiving reef, so transport did not resolve within-reef flows; a finer-scale hydrodynamic network is under development and was not used here. The working COTS formulation combined preferred-first per-capita grazing, survival linked to remembered preferred coral cover, adult senescence and preferred-food effects on reproductive condition. Larval production included a low-density Allee effect and juvenile survival a saturating predator-pit term. External larval supply was derived from a reef-level outbreak-probability hindcast [@stewart2026hybrid]; its production multiplier was a calibration assumption. Coral thermal responses, a chlorophyll-based larval-survival modifier and wave-exposure effects on settlement were included in the working configuration [@adriacalibrationreport2026]. Simulated adult density was converted to manta CPUE through a linear observation model with 0.015 COTS tow$^{-1}$ per adult ha$^{-1}$.

Calibration compared outbreak timing, size, troughs and coral change on the four monitoring reefs, using `r int(mcn("base_seeds"))` base seed pairs plus twelve one-at-a-time parameter perturbations of ±25%, giving `r int(mcn("calibration_arms_per_cull_state"))` runs in each culling state. Bands across these runs are not probability intervals. Calibration scoring kept culling off, and paired runs applied recorded removals. Recorded cull totals were distributed among sites on the same reef in proportion to simulated population, retaining juvenile and adult stages and pre- and post-spawning timing, and were capped at the animals available.

Five further Long-Term Monitoring Program reefs in the domain were simulated but excluded from the calibration score. Martin and Linnet have outbreak histories; Yonge, Carter and No Name have recorded at most 0.01 COTS per tow. A preregistered check on these reefs found false outbreaks on the last three. We then added a time-invariant settlement multiplier on reefs with a mean peak wave period above 6.6 s, falling linearly to 0.25 at 7.0 s, with limits taken from monitoring records on 29 domain reefs that include these three. Martin and Linnet are unaffected by the multiplier and so give the more independent check. Simulated series were compared with manta records and with a no-model baseline, the mean observed series of the four calibration reefs.

Exploratory projections to 2050 used `r int(mcn("climate_models"))` climate models, five seed pairs, two climate pathways (SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0) and nine culling levels, giving `r int(mcn("projection_arms"))` runs. Historical catches applied through 2026 and effort-based culling from 2027, with density-dependent catch rates capped by the available population. Increased effort multiplied recent diver-hours on each reef; targeted effort reallocated the same total among reefs with at least 3 adults per hectare. Vessel travel and search costs were not represented.

## Software and reproducibility

The SDM analyses used R 4.5.0 with xgboost, Hmsc and terra, and the metacommunity model used COTSMod.jl within ADRIA [@cotsmodmethods2026; @adriamethods2026]. Inputs were pinned by SHA-256 checksum, and all reported results were read from output tables when the manuscript was rendered. [TO CONFIRM: package versions and frozen code releases, with DOIs, for the R pipeline, COTSMod.jl and ADRIA.]

# Results

## Habitat models rank locations within a reef only weakly

Habitat gave only a weak first order to places on a reef. Across the GBR, the values of the habitat layers mostly reflected region and survey year, whereas within a reef the 30 m layers varied over tens of meters (@fig-study). On all four example reefs, from Eyrie in the north to Lady Musgrave in the south, the cull-trained layers ranked reef margins and outer slopes highest (@fig-maps). Measured against manta tows that none of the layers had been fitted to, the best cull-trained layer (RG + year) placed strong-evidence tows above clean tows only slightly more often than chance (within reef-year AUC `r ci3(mi("RG + year", "within_reef_year_auc"), mi("RG + year", "auc_low"), mi("RG + year", "auc_high"))`; @tbl-tows). Clean + year was barely better than random (`r a3(mi("Clean + year", "within_reef_year_auc"))`). A habitat model trained on the tows themselves ranked held-out tows best (`r a3(mt("within", "auc"))`), and its strongest predictors were wave period, wave height, depth and slope. The layers also disagreed on detail. Within a reef, the rankings of any two layers correlated at only `r a2(min(la$median))`–`r a2(max(la$median))` (median Spearman correlations; Supplementary Table S6), and the two cull-trained layers at `r a2(fbc$spearman)` where both existed. These patterns indicate that habitat can give a first search order on a reef that crews know little about, but cannot by itself justify leaving ground unsearched.

![**The habitat layers agree on reef margins and outer slopes but differ in detail.** Within-reef percentile rank of each layer on Eyrie, Batt, Big Broadhurst and Lady Musgrave reefs (rows): clean + year, RG + year, the manta model, joint-model (HMSC) habitat and the joint model updated with cull history, each at its delivered resolution (30 m, or 120 m for the joint model). Color resolves the top 30% of each reef, from the 70th percentile (dark purple) to the highest-ranked cells (yellow). The last column is the width of the joint model's 90% posterior interval, darker where it is wider. RG + year and the manta model are blank where ReefGuidance layers are missing.](../outputs/figures/fig02_four_reef_comparison.png){#fig-maps width="100%"}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tows
#| tbl-cap: "Discrimination between strong-evidence and strictly negative manta tows within reef-years. Upper rows: independent check of the deployed habitat layers, none of which used manta tows. Lower rows: cull-trained and manta-trained models refitted on the same leave-reef-out folds and scored on held-out reefs. Lift is the share of strong-evidence tows in a reef-year's top 20%, divided by 20%. Brackets: 95% bootstrap intervals over reef-years."
fmt <- function(e, l, h, f = a3) sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", f(e), f(l), f(h))
mods <- c(cull = "Cull-trained (RG predictors + year)", manta = "Manta-trained (with year)", within = "Manta-trained, within reef-year")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Model = c(paste0(mic$layer, " (deployed layer)"), unname(mods)),
  Tows = c(int(mic$tows), vapply(names(mods), function(m) int(mt(m, "auc", "tows")), "")),
  `Within reef-year AUC` = c(fmt(mic$within_reef_year_auc, mic$auc_low, mic$auc_high),
                             vapply(names(mods), function(m) fmt(mt(m, "auc"), mt(m, "auc", "low"), mt(m, "auc", "high")), "")),
  `Top-20% lift` = c(fmt(mic$top20_lift, mic$lift_low, mic$lift_high, a2),
                     vapply(names(mods), function(m) fmt(mt(m, "lift"), mt(m, "lift", "low"), mt(m, "lift", "high"), a2), "")),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrll")
```

## Cull history forecasts problematic sites but encodes where crews dive

Problematic sites persisted from one season to the next, so the places where crews had culled COTS before were the best guide to where they would cull them again. Scored strictly forward in time, a blend of habitat and cull history ranked problematic site-years at a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(fvh("combined_fixed"), fvh("combined_fixed", col = "auc_low"), fvh("combined_fixed", col = "auc_high"))`, against `r a3(fvh("habitat"))` for habitat alone (@tbl-forward). Much of that skill came from the crews rather than the starfish. A score built only on how often crews had dived a site reached `r a3(fvh("effort"))`, and the blend fell from `r a3(fvh("combined_fixed", "with nearby history"))` where history lay nearby to `r a3(fvh("combined_fixed", "new sites"))` at sites never culled before. History is also sparse, reaching only `r p1(hist$fraction_with_history)` of 120 m reef cells. Put simply, cull history is a map of past finds that is valuable for briefing crews, but it says little about ground they have not yet searched.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forward
#| tbl-cap: "Forward validation of scores for problematic cull site-years: within reef-year AUC, test years 2022–2026 pooled. Every score uses only data from before the test year. History settings were fixed before validation. Sample sizes are site-years."
meth <- c(habitat = "Habitat (joint model refitted before test year)", habitat_context = "Habitat + reef context",
          effort = "Dive effort only", history_fixed = "History kernel", combined_fixed = "Habitat + history")
subs <- c("all", "with nearby history", "little or no nearby history", "new sites")
tf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(meth), function(m) {
  v <- vapply(subs, function(s) a3(fvh(m, s)), "")
  v[1] <- fmt(fvh(m), fvh(m, col = "auc_low"), fvh(m, col = "auc_high"))
  data.frame(Score = meth[[m]], t(v), check.names = FALSE)
}))
names(tf)[-1] <- sprintf("%s (n = %s)", c("All (95% CI)", "Nearby history", "Little or none", "New sites"),
                         vapply(subs, function(s) int(fvh("habitat", s, col = "site_years")), ""))
knitr::kable(tf, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")
```

## Evenly spaced manta tows retain more aggregations than model-ranked tows

Spreading the kept tows evenly around a reef found more aggregations than any ranking, at every level of effort (@fig-aggregations). With 60% of tows kept, evenly spaced (systematic) thinning still found `r p1(ag(0.6, "systematic"))` of `r int(ag(0.6, "aggregations"))` aggregations in `r int(ag(0.6, "surveys"))` surveys, random thinning found `r p1(ag(0.6, "random"))`, and thinning by the held-out cull-trained layer found `r cip(ag(0.6, "layer_cv"), ag(0.6, "layer_cv_low"), ag(0.6, "layer_cv_high"))`. Put another way, systematic thinning could drop `r p0(mx("systematic_point"))` of tows and still find 95% of aggregations, whereas the layer could drop only `r p0(mx("layer_cv_point"))`. Even the manta model, which ranked individual tows best, found fewer aggregations than random (`r p1(pick(mra, strategy = "random", keep = 0.6, col = "found"))`) or systematic thinning (`r p1(pick(mra, strategy = "systematic", keep = 0.6, col = "found"))`). A ranking keeps tows on a few high-scoring stretches of reef, so an aggregation on a low-scoring stretch loses every tow, whereas even spacing leaves a tow near almost every aggregation. Scoring the tows with the in-sample layer would have overstated aggregations found by `r pp(ag(0.6, "layer_deployed") - ag(0.6, "layer_cv"))` percentage points. These patterns indicate that rankings should direct additional tows, not decide which tows to drop.

![**Spreading manta tows evenly finds more COTS aggregations than keeping the highest-ranked tows.** (**a**) Share of aggregations (two or more strong-evidence tows within 500 m in one survey) still found as tows are cut within each survey, for evenly spaced thinning (black squares), random thinning (grey triangles, dashed) and thinning by the cull-trained habitat layer (orange), either held out by reef (filled circles, with a 95% bootstrap band over surveys) or scored in-sample (open circles, dashed). An aggregation counts as found if any of its tows is kept; the dotted line marks 95%. (**b**) Share found with 60% of tows kept, by the number of strong-evidence tows in the aggregation; a single tow is an isolated record.](../outputs/figures/fig13_manta_aggregation_cv.png){#fig-aggregations width="100%"}

## Recent evidence improves cull-site selection, with limits at high retention

Used alone, habitat sorted designated sites little better than chance. Searching the top 70% of sites by the held-out habitat layer retained `r cip(cs("problematic_dives_kept", 0.7), cs("problematic_dives_kept", 0.7, col = "low"), cs("problematic_dives_kept", 0.7, col = "high"))` of problematic dives, where a ranking with no information would retain `r p1(cs("dives_kept", 0.7))`. Adding the previous season's dives and tows shortened the search. Over 2018–2026 (`r int(ev_dives)` dives in `r int(ev_ry)` reef-years), keeping 90% of problematic dives required `r p0(ev("sites_searched", 0.9, "habitat"))` of designated sites with habitat alone but `r p0(ev("sites_searched", 0.9, "combined"))` with recent evidence added, and every paired interval excluded zero. Most of that saving came from moving quiet and never-dived sites down the list. Among dives that crews actually made, the ranking separated problematic from low-density dives only slightly better than habitat alone (AUC `r a2(pick(eauc, window = "last_season", subset = "all", score = "combined", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))` against `r a2(pick(eauc, window = "last_season", subset = "all", score = "habitat", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))`). Recent evidence therefore helps mostly by telling crews where not to look first.

Fitted only on earlier seasons, the ranking needed a few years of records before it helped. It avoided more low-density dives than habitat alone in every season from 2022 and searched fewer sites in every season from 2023, but not in 2019–2021 (Supplementary Table S7). Judged against the management target over 2019–2026 (`r int(fw_dives)` dives in `r int(fw_ry)` reef-years), keeping 90% of dives above 0.04 required `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.9)` of designated sites, against `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.9, "habitat"))` with habitat alone and `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.9, "random"))` at random (@tbl-site-rule, @fig-high-density). The savings shrank quickly as the tolerance for misses tightened, and keeping 99% of such dives required `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.99))` of sites. The acceptable rate of missed high-density dives is therefore a management choice, and it sets how much search the ranking can save.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-site-rule
#| tbl-cap: "Cull sites selected and low-density or ghost dives avoided, 2019–2026. Upper rows fix retention of dives above 0.04 CPUE; final rows fix the A–D site count and report retention. Percentages with 95% reef-year bootstrap intervals in brackets. Sites are candidate site-years, including never-dived sites. Low-density means positive CPUE below 0.02."
highlight_rows <- expand.grid(target = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99), score = c("habitat", "combined", "random"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
highlight_rows <- highlight_rows[order(highlight_rows$target, highlight_rows$score), ]
highlight_metric <- function(metric) vapply(seq_len(nrow(highlight_rows)), function(i) {
  x <- highlight_rows[i, ]
  sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", 100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score), 100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, col = "low"), 100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, col = "high"))
}, character(1))
highlight_table <- data.frame(
  `Retained above 0.04 (%)` = as.character(100 * highlight_rows$target),
  Ranking = c(combined = "Habitat + recent evidence", habitat = "Habitat alone", random = "Random")[highlight_rows$score],
  `Sites selected (%)` = highlight_metric("sites_searched"),
  `Low-density avoided (%)` = highlight_metric("low_avoided"),
  `Ghost avoided (%)` = highlight_metric("ghost_avoided"),
  check.names = FALSE)
opsc <- c("combined", "habitat", "random")
opcell <- function(metric) vapply(opsc, function(s) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", 100 * oc(metric, s), 100 * oc(metric, s, "low"), 100 * oc(metric, s, "high")), "")
operational_rows <- data.frame(opcell("high_retained"), c("A–D: habitat + recent evidence", "A–D count: habitat alone", "A–D count: random"),
  opcell("sites_selected"), opcell("low_avoided"), opcell("ghost_avoided"), check.names = FALSE)
names(operational_rows) <- names(highlight_table)
knitr::kable(rbind(highlight_table, operational_rows), row.names = FALSE)
```

![**Recent evidence keeps more high-density dives for the same search, but savings shrink as retention tightens.** Share of dives above 0.04 COTS per minute kept against the share of designated site-years searched, 2019–2026, for habitat alone (orange), habitat plus the previous season's cull dives and manta tows (blue), and random selection of the same number of sites on each reef (grey, dashed). Bands are 95% reef-year bootstrap intervals; dotted lines mark 80, 90, 95 and 99% retention, and the diamond marks the A–D class cut-off. Habitat fits were held out by reef, and the evidence regression used only earlier seasons.](../outputs/figures/fig20_high_density_retention.png){#fig-high-density width="100%"}

As a fixed rule on every site, the ranking mostly protected productive dives rather than avoiding empty ones. Retaining classes A–D selected `r p1(oc("sites_selected"))` of sites and kept `r occi("high_retained")` of dives above 0.04, against `r p1(oc("high_retained", "random"))` for the same number of sites chosen at random. It avoided no more low-density dives than random selection (`r p1(oc("low_avoided"))` against `r p1(oc("low_avoided", "random"))`), and a similar share of ghost dives (`r p1(oc("ghost_avoided"))` against `r p1(oc("ghost_avoided", "random"))`). Because it kept repeatedly visited, productive sites, it also deferred fewer of the dives crews actually made (`r p1(od("all_dives_avoided"))` against `r p1(od("all_dives_avoided", "random"))` at random). A rule applied to every site therefore guards the dives that matter most, but does little about the empty dives that cost the program time.

Part of this gain reproduces what crews already know. Refreshing the evidence to each voyage's departure selected `r num(100 * abs(dvdv("fwd_voyage", "sites_at_90_04")), 1)` percentage points fewer sites at 90% retention than evidence from the previous season (95% CI `r num(100 * abs(dvdv("fwd_voyage", "sites_at_90_04", "high")), 1)`–`r num(100 * abs(dvdv("fwd_voyage", "sites_at_90_04", "low")), 1)`), reflecting the value of finds made earlier in the same season. Crews already dive open sites first, and those sites held `r p0(mzp("open", "high") / ptot$high)` of dives above 0.04 in the replay. None of three pre-specified alternatives replaced the ranking. Counting any earlier dive above 0.04 as the site trigger made little difference (`r p1(rk("dives_avoided", "high_indicator"))` of dives avoided, against `r p1(rk("dives_avoided", "archived"))`). Neither recency-weighted site CPUE (a paired gain of `r rdci("dives_avoided")` percentage points) nor ranking sites by the best-valued part of their habitat improved on it.

## Ranking only weak-evidence dives avoids more empty dives

Ranking only the dives that crews make on weak evidence avoided far more empty dives for each one missed. On the same `r int(ptot$visits)` visits, the site rule and the workflow skipped similar shares of dives (`r p1(ps(SR, "dives_avoided_pct"))` and `r p1(ps(WF, "dives_avoided_pct"))`), with very different consequences (@tbl-workflow). The site rule missed `r p1(ps(SR, "high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04 and avoided `r p1(ps(SR, "ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives, whereas the workflow missed `r psci(WF, "high_missed_pct")` and avoided `r p1(ps(WF, "ghost_avoided_pct"))`. That is `r num(ps(WF, "ghost_per_high_missed"), 1)` ghost dives avoided for each missed dive above 0.04, about twice the `r num(ps(RWF, "ghost_per_high_missed"), 1)` achieved by skipping the same number of dives at random. Low-density dives were avoided at close to the random rate (`r p1(ps(WF, "low_avoided_pct"))` against `r p1(ps(RWF, "low_avoided_pct"))`). The missed dives were mostly marginal, with a median CPUE of `r num(ps(WF, "cpue_missed_high_median"), 3)` against a mean of `r num(ptot$cpue_high_mean, 3)` for all dives above 0.04, and together held `r p1(ps(WF, "cots_forgone_pct"))` of the COTS culled. Put simply, the workflow trades a small number of near-threshold dives for a large reduction in dives that find nothing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-workflow
#| tbl-cap: "Workflow settings replayed on 2019–2026 reef visits. Percentages are of all tows made and of all ghost, low-density and above-0.04 dives under current practice. 'Ghost per miss' is ghost dives avoided per dive above 0.04 missed. The random row skips the same number of dives at random among those without strong evidence."
wf_rows <- c("Site rule A–D, all dives" = SR, "Evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives" = "evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives",
             "Dive rule A–D" = "dive rule A-D", "Dive rule A–C" = WF, "Same number as A–C, at random" = RWF, "Dive rule A–B" = "dive rule A-B",
             "Tow zone with season memory" = "zone with season memory", "Dive rule A–C + tow zone" = WFZ)
has_ps <- function(v, m) any(pst$variant == v & pst$metric == m & pst$scope == "all visits")
cellp <- function(v, m) if (has_ps(v, m)) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * ps(v, m)) else "—"
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Setting = names(wf_rows),
  `Tows saved (%)` = vapply(wf_rows, cellp, "", m = "tows_saved_pct"),
  `Dives skipped (%)` = vapply(wf_rows, cellp, "", m = "dives_avoided_pct"),
  `Ghost avoided (%)` = vapply(wf_rows, cellp, "", m = "ghost_avoided_pct"),
  `Low-density avoided (%)` = vapply(wf_rows, cellp, "", m = "low_avoided_pct"),
  `Above 0.04 missed (%)` = vapply(wf_rows, cellp, "", m = "high_missed_pct"),
  `Ghost per miss` = vapply(wf_rows, function(v) if (has_ps(v, "ghost_per_high_missed")) num(ps(v, "ghost_per_high_missed"), 1) else "—", ""),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Most empty dives followed weak evidence, which is where a ranking can help. Of all ghost dives, `r p0(mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "ghost") / ptot$ghost)` were at sites whose nearest tows showed at most a single feeding scar. Evidence alone could not separate these empty dives from productive ones. Simply not diving on weak evidence avoided `r p0(ps("evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives", "ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives but missed `r p1(ps("evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives", "high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04, because `r p0(mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "high") / mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "dives"))` of weak-scar dives exceeded the target. The ranking's contribution was to choose which of those dives to skip, using each site's habitat and recent record.

On follow-up visits, towing only the A–C zone saved boat time with few misses. Under within-reef classes it saved `r p0(mza("follow-up", "zone", "tows_saved") / mza("follow-up", "zone", "tows"))` of follow-up tows and missed `r int(mza("follow-up", "zone", "high_lost"))` dives above 0.04 over eight seasons. Skipping the same tows at random positions missed `r int(round(mza("follow-up", "shifted", "high_lost")))`, and blocks of nine tows on and three off, which saved `r p0(mza("follow-up", "block", "tows_saved", ranking = "9on3off") / mza("follow-up", "block", "tows", ranking = "9on3off"))` of tows, missed `r int(round(mza("follow-up", "block", "high_lost", ranking = "9on3off")))`. Keeping sites near strong tows from earlier in the season ("season memory") cut the misses to `r int(ps("zone with season memory", "high_missed"))` while saving `r p0(ps("zone with season memory", "tows_saved_follow_up_pct"))` of follow-up tows. On first visits of a season, however, the zone missed more dives than block thinning. The zone is therefore proposed only between full sweeps of a reef.

## Density-aware classes avoid more empty dives for each miss

Letting the share of high-priority sites follow each reef's recent density avoided more empty dives for the same misses (@tbl-density, @fig-ghost-per-miss). Scored forward on `r int(pdtot$visits)` visits over 2020–2026, the second density-aware version avoided `r p1(dlmv(V2, "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"))` of ghost dives at the point where 3% of dives above 0.04 were missed, against `r p1(dlmv("density-aware", "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"))` for the first version (`r dlmd(V2, "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed")`) and `r p1(dlmv("within-reef", "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"))` for within-reef classes. The second version corrected reefs whose recent records contradicted their earlier history. Big Broadhurst, where `r int(v2rv("18-100a", "problematic_dives_12m"))` of `r int(v2rv("18-100a", "dives_12m"))` dives in the past year were problematic but most came from the mid-2025 voyages, fell from a density of `r num(v2rv("18-100a", "reef_density_v1"), 2)` under the first version to `r num(v2rv("18-100a", "reef_density_v2"), 2)`. John Brewer, where `r int(v2rv("18-075", "tows_12m"))` tows in the past year found no strong evidence, fell from `r num(v2rv("18-075", "reef_density_v1"), 2)` to `r num(v2rv("18-075", "reef_density_v2"), 2)`. Rules based on tow evidence alone did no better than skipping dives at random, whereas every class-based rule did better. The second version's classes are stricter, so the same cut-off skips more dives. At A–D it avoided `r p1(pdv(V2, "none", "A-D", "ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives and missed `r int(pdv(V2, "none", "A-D", "high_missed"))` dives above 0.04, and at A–C `r p1(pdv(V2, "none", "A-C", "ghost_avoided_pct"))` and `r int(pdv(V2, "none", "A-C", "high_missed"))` (Supplementary Table S8).

The recommended setting combines the second version with a dive rule at A–D and a follow-up tow zone at A–C. The dive rule avoided `r cri("ghost_avoided_pct")` of ghost dives and missed `r p1(crv("high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04, or `r num(crv("ghost_per_high_missed"), 1)` ghost dives avoided per miss, against `r num(crd("ghost_per_high_missed"), 1)` when the same number of dives was skipped at random. On follow-up visits, the zone saved `r czi("zone_saved_pct")` of tows and missed `r int(czb("zone_lost"))` dives above 0.04, where skipping the same tows at other positions missed about `r num(czb("shifted_lost"), 0)`. Together, the two rules missed `r int(ccv("high_missed"))` dives above 0.04 over seven seasons, `r p1(ccv("high_missed_pct"))` of those recorded.

Ground that tows had long found clean remained a poor guide on dense reefs. On test visits to reefs denser than typical, sites with at least five tows and no strong scar or dive in the previous one to six years were `r p0(dclv("problematic"))` problematic when dived (`r int(dclv("dives"))` dives). Batt Reef's north-eastern flank is an example. Since 2019, only `r p1(bflv(V2, "strong_share", "NE"))` of its `r int(bflv(V2, "tows_since_2019", "NE"))` tows found strong evidence, against `r p1(bflv(V2, "strong_share", "SW"))` on the south-western flank, yet the second version still places `r int(bflv(V2, "a_to_c", "NE"))` of its `r int(bflv(V2, "sites", "NE"))` sites in A–C. On reefs like Batt, this season's tows, through the tow zone and season memory, are a better guide than a clean record from earlier years.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-density
#| tbl-cap: "Class sets compared at matched effort, 2020–2026 replay. Each set's dive-rule and tow-zone results are interpolated to a common point. Ghost and low-density dives avoided are read where 3% of dives above 0.04 are missed. Dives above 0.04 missed are read where 14% of dives are skipped. Zone misses are dives above 0.04 lost where 12% of follow-up tows are saved. Brackets: 95% bootstrap interval over reef-years."
dl_rows <- c(`Within-reef` = "within-reef", `Density-aware, first version` = "density-aware", `Density-aware, second version` = V2)
ci_txt <- function(l, m, scale = 100, d = 1) sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", num(scale * dlmv(l, m), d), num(scale * dlmv(l, m, "low"), d), num(scale * dlmv(l, m, "high"), d))
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Class set` = names(dl_rows),
                        `Ghost avoided (%)` = vapply(dl_rows, ci_txt, "", m = "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"),
                        `Low-density avoided (%)` = vapply(dl_rows, ci_txt, "", m = "low_avoided_at_3pct_missed"),
                        `Above 0.04 missed (%)` = vapply(dl_rows, ci_txt, "", m = "high_missed_at_14pct_skipped", d = 2),
                        `Zone misses` = vapply(dl_rows, ci_txt, "", m = "zone_missed_at_12pct_tows_saved", scale = 1),
                        check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
```

![**Class-based dive rules avoid more empty dives for each high-density dive missed than rules based on tow evidence alone.** Ghost dives avoided per dive above 0.04 COTS per minute missed in the 2020–2026 replay, for rules based on tow evidence alone (dark grey), the same number of dives skipped at random (light grey; dashed line), and dive rules at the stated class cut-off under within-reef (blue), first density-aware (purple) and second density-aware (green) classes, alone and with the follow-up tow zone. Dive rules apply to dives without a strong tow within 100 m. Whiskers are 95% intervals over 300 reef-year resamples; outlined bars are the three options with the highest ratio. Supplementary Table S8 gives the dives missed by each setting.](../outputs/figures/fig34_ghost_per_miss.png){#fig-ghost-per-miss width="100%"}

## Products for the 2027 season

The 2027 products give every designated site a class and every reef a place to explore. Of the `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs, `r int(v2cl("all reefs", "density_v2_a"))` are class A and `r int(v2cl("all reefs", "density_v2_a_to_c"))` are A–C under the second density-aware version. A further `r int(n_noev)` sites (`r p0(n_noev / nrow(pri))`) lie on reefs with no dives or tows in the evidence window, where habitat and the reef-level forecast set the order. Exploration zones cover `r int(nrow(expz_band(0.6)))` reefs in their broadest band, with a median of `r num(median(expz_band(0.6)$area_ha), 0)` ha per reef. Historically, tows on new ground, with no tow within 300 m in the previous five seasons, recorded strong evidence more often than repeat tows (`r p1(eg("new ground", "cull", "strong_share"))` against `r p1(eg("repeat ground", "cull", "strong_share"))`). This may partly reflect outbreak stage, because new ground is often surveyed early in an outbreak, and the zones themselves have not been trialed. They nevertheless give crews somewhere to look beyond the sites that past effort keeps returning them to.

## Metacommunity calibration and exploratory projections

The metacommunity model reproduced the broad sequence of historical outbreak waves, and of coral decline and recovery, on Lizard Island, Eyrie, MacGillivray and North Direction reefs (@fig-metacommunity), but not every detail. Lizard Island's first peak remained too small, and modeled coral cover departed from surveys in some periods. The model captured the build-up of the fifth primary outbreak wave but overshot observed densities on several reefs, which could understate the relative effect of recent culling. Because the corrected outbreak inputs and the recent-density targets drew on the same cull and diver evidence, this recent comparison is a diagnostic rather than a test.

![**The metacommunity model reproduces the broad sequence of outbreak waves and coral change on the calibration reefs.** (**a**, **c**, **e**, **g**) COTS per manta tow and (**b**, **d**, **f**, **h**) hard coral cover, modeled relative to habitable area, on Lizard Island, MacGillivray, North Direction and Eyrie reefs. Lines are five-seed means without recorded culling (sky blue, solid) and with it (vermillion, dashed). Darker bands span the five seeds and lighter bands span all 65 parameter-test runs in each culling state; they are not confidence intervals. Black points are Long-Term Monitoring Program manta observations, grey diamonds are 9 m photo-transects, and the dotted line marks 0.22 COTS per tow. These are calibration and diagnostic comparisons.](../outputs/figures/fig22_metacommunity_cots_coral.png){#fig-metacommunity width="100%"}

Outside its calibration, the model timed outbreak peaks well but sized them poorly (@tbl-extra, @fig-extra). It placed the Martin and Linnet peaks of the 1990s in `r cpkv("Martin Reef", "1990s", "model_peak_year")` and `r cpkv("Linnet Reef", "1990s", "model_peak_year")`, against observed peaks in `r cpkv("Martin Reef", "1990s", "obs_peak_year")` and `r cpkv("Linnet Reef", "1990s", "obs_peak_year")`, and both 2010s peaks in `r cpkv("Martin Reef", "2010s", "model_peak_year")`, against `r cpkv("Martin Reef", "2010s", "obs_peak_year")`. Its peaks in the 2010s were too low. It ordered survey years better than the no-model baseline but was not consistently better at identifying outbreak years, being worse on Martin and having a higher mean absolute error on Linnet. Before the wave-exposure term was added, the model produced false outbreaks on Yonge, Carter and No Name, peaking at 0.33–0.48 COTS per tow with five to seven years at or above 0.22. With the term, they stayed below 0.1 COTS per tow, with almost no change to the calibration score. Because the term was designed from those records, this agreement checks the design and does not validate it.

<!-- Pre-wave values: COTSMod-Calibration store/runs/20261019T_04_extra_reefs_w2_1991_v1,
extra_reefs_audit.csv, linear detection. -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-extra
#| tbl-cap: "Model against Long-Term Monitoring Program manta records, 1992–2026, on reefs outside the calibration score, for five-seed means without culling. The baseline is the mean observed series of the four calibration reefs. MAE: mean absolute error in COTS per tow. TSS: true skill statistic for years at or above 0.22 COTS per tow, undefined where no such year was observed. Spearman is undefined on No Name, which recorded no COTS. The wave-exposure term was designed using Yonge, Carter and No Name."
ar_f <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(is.finite(x), num(x, d), "—")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Reef = sub(" Reef", "", car$reef),
  `Max, obs. / model` = sprintf("%s / %s", ar_f(car$obs_max_cpue), ar_f(car$model_max_cpue)),
  `Years ≥0.22, obs. / model` = sprintf("%d / %d", car$obs_years_irruption, car$model_years_irruption),
  `MAE, model / base` = sprintf("%s / %s", ar_f(car$mae, 3), ar_f(car$baseline_mae, 3)),
  `Spearman, model / base` = sprintf("%s / %s", ar_f(car$spearman), ar_f(car$baseline_spearman)),
  `TSS, model / base` = sprintf("%s / %s", ar_f(car$tss), ar_f(car$baseline_tss)),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "llllll")
```

![**Outside its calibration, the model timed outbreak peaks well but sized them poorly.** COTS per manta tow on (**a**) Martin, (**b**) Linnet, (**c**) Yonge, (**d**) Carter, (**e**) No Name and (**f**) Ribbon No 10 reefs, which were simulated but not used in the calibration score. Lines and bands as in @fig-metacommunity. Black points are Long-Term Monitoring Program manta observations (Ribbon No 10 has no monitoring series), and the dotted line marks 0.22 COTS per tow.](../outputs/figures/fig24_metacommunity_additional_reefs.png){#fig-extra width="100%"}

In exploratory scenarios to 2050, increased effort lowered near-term COTS peaks, with coral outcomes that varied among reefs and climate pathways (@fig-projection). Reallocating the same effort among reefs could increase domain-wide removals without giving the largest benefit at the five reefs shown. Excess simulated COTS in 2026 carry into these near-term projections, so the scenarios show what the model can compare, not the outcomes managers should expect.

# Discussion

Fine-scale models improved search decisions only when they were joined to the information crews already use. Our results indicate four key findings. Firstly, habitat alone ranked places on a reef weakly, so it can give crews a first search order on an unfamiliar reef but cannot justify leaving ground unsearched. Secondly, a ranking applied to every designated site mainly protected productive dives, because much of its skill restates where crews have found COTS before. Thirdly, the same ranking applied only to dives made on weak evidence, with class shares scaled to each reef's recent density, avoided about `r num(crv("ghost_per_high_missed"), 0)` empty dives for every high-density dive missed, against about `r num(crd("ghost_per_high_missed"), 0)` when dives were skipped at random. Fourthly, evenly spaced manta tows kept more aggregations than any model-ranked selection. The metacommunity strand has reached an earlier stage. It reproduces important features of past outbreaks and can compare effort scenarios, but its results are not yet estimates of management benefit.

## Where a ranking adds value in daily operations

A key learning is that a ranking is most useful where crews have the least to go on, not where they already know COTS are. Applied to every site, it deferred dives that crews would have made on strong evidence, and its low-density avoidance was no better than random. Most ghost dives instead followed weak evidence, such as a single feeding scar or only negative tows nearby. This is the part of the decision that a ranking can inform, because it brings a site's habitat and recent record to a choice that a fixed scar threshold cannot make well. Indeed, a two-scar trigger avoided many empty dives but missed too many above the management target, which confirms a concern the program had already raised from its own analysis of feeding-scar records. Put simply, the ranking does not tell crews where COTS are; it helps them decide which uncertain dives to leave.

Habitat and recent observations have complementary coverage. Habitat layers describe reef settings everywhere, including places crews have rarely searched, whereas dives and tows give direct evidence of current populations but only where crews have looked. Static terrain and coral habitat cannot describe the stage of an outbreak, recent removals or the movement of aggregations, which is consistent with reef-level studies showing the importance of connectivity and of conditions associated with outbreak development [@matthews2020connectivity; @stewart2026hybrid]. Habitat therefore matters most on the reefs, and the parts of reefs, that crews visit least, which is where the exploration zones point them.

The ranking also captures operator behavior. Crews select sites using previous observations and their knowledge of the reef, so a model trained on their records partly formalizes those choices, as expected for preferentially collected observations [@diggle2010preferential; @phillips2009bias]. Most dives above 0.04 were at open sites that crews already dive first, and evidence refreshed to voyage departure largely reproduces what crews know when they leave port. The savings measured against random selection should therefore not be read as savings against current practice. The workflow replay is the fairer test, because it keeps the triggers crews use.

Density-aware classes address a structural weakness of within-reef ranks, which give a nearly empty reef as many high-priority sites as a reef in active outbreak. Much of their gain came from moving effort between reefs. Their design also shows the limits of learning from past effort. The first version, fitted only to reefs that crews had dived, kept reefs towed clean through the past year, such as John Brewer, too high, and held a reef such as Big Broadhurst at the density of its busiest voyages months after the starfish had been culled down. Weighting recent records more heavily and counting tow-only surveys corrected both. Untowed ground also needed a neutral treatment, so that it neither outranked towed ground with strong scars nor dropped out of consideration. Exploration zones respond to the same concern, because rankings learned from past effort otherwise keep consolidating search on the same places, and their value should be tested by recording nil results as well as finds.

## Maintaining spatial coverage in manta surveillance

The manta results show why retaining high-scoring individual observations differs from retaining detections of whole aggregations. Model-ranked thinning concentrated observations in favored areas and left aggregations elsewhere vulnerable to being missed. On first visits of a season, coverage should therefore take priority. The follow-up tow zone is a narrower use of ranking, applied between full sweeps and only with memory of earlier strong tows. It saves boat time but avoids few empty dives. These comparisons concern retrospective thinning of existing surveys. Tow sequence was inferred from position, and new routes remain untested, so future records should capture actual tow order and vessel time.

## Limits of retrospective replay

The replay can only re-score dives that crews chose to make, and cannot show what undived sites held. A dive was counted as missed whenever its only strong tow was skipped, although crews might have dived there anyway. COTS at a skipped site remain until the next visit, so COTS forgone overstates any lasting loss, while a delay can still allow coral to be eaten. Tows saved count tows, not vessel time. The recommended cut-offs and the weight on the visit model were chosen on the same seasons used for testing, so the margins between closely ranked options are somewhat optimistic. In the forward test the habitat fits were held out by reef but not restricted to earlier years, and the reef-level forecasts before 2026 were probably fitted on the same years. Validation should match the spatial and temporal decision being supported [@roberts2017cv], and discrimination should be assessed within reefs [@lobo2008auc].

These limits define what a field trial must measure. A median voyage held only `r int(cpv("flagged"))` dive`r if (cpv("flagged") == 1) "" else "s"` that the A–D rule would skip, so a single voyage can test usability and towing time but not the rule's effect. Recording what the rule would have done on every voyage, with the ranking frozen at departure and without changing operations, would give a `r p0(cpt(25))` chance of detecting the expected difference after 25 voyages. Field trials planned for early 2027 will compare the rules with normal crew planning. Deferred sites still need annual or pre-closure checks, and those checks, repeat dives and exploration must all be counted before any annual saving is claimed.

## A platform for strategic comparisons

The metacommunity strand addresses a different management scale: how culling on one reef affects COTS and coral there and on connected reefs. Reef-scale models have established the importance of comparing control strategies under interacting disturbances [@morello2014model; @condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative]. The present prototype adds site resolution within a framework that can run large scenario ensembles [@matthews2020cotsmod; @adriamethods2026]. Its calibration remains in-sample, and peak sizes, densities between waves and the recent build-up depend on coral assumptions and on the relationship between manta observations and true abundance. The reefs outside the calibration give partial support. Timing on Martin and Linnet was close, but outbreak waves are regionally synchronous and external larval supply came from a reef-level hindcast, so correct timing is a modest test. The false outbreaks on outer reefs exposed a structural gap that a wave-exposure term closed. That term remains to be tested on reefs not used in its design, and wave period also marks outer-shelf position, so it cannot separate exposure from other outer-shelf properties such as low chlorophyll.

Two questions need this framework once it is validated. The first is the program's impact since 2012, which requires paired histories from the same population and coral state with and without recorded removals. Holding outside larval supply constant estimates the effect of control inside the model domain only; a regional counterfactual needs outside supply consistent with no control on those reefs. The second is whether the fifth primary outbreak wave can be suppressed, and at what cost. A reef with little coral left to protect may still supply larvae to neighbors, and fewer COTS need not yield lasting coral gains if heat stress or cyclones remove the spared coral, so scenarios must follow larval export and downstream coral as well as local catches. Effort, detection as COTS become scarce, and vessel travel must also be represented before starting and stopping rules can describe operational choices credibly.

## Conclusion

Recent observations combined with habitat, applied where crews have the least to go on, offer a testable way to reduce empty dives at program scale while keeping most high-density dives. The test against crew practice remains to be done in the field. The metacommunity model provides a platform for asking how those removals change outbreaks and coral across connected reefs, but does not yet establish the coral benefit of any control strategy. For reef interventions more generally, the results show the value of evaluating decision support within the decision it is meant to change, against what operators would do without it. Every empty dive avoided returns diver time to reefs where sustained culling protects coral [@westcott2020efficacy; @matthews2024protecting], and in a warming climate that protection helps buy time for reefs between disturbances.
